section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distribution
section_1.content: Briefly define a probability distribution. Introduce the 'Uniform Distribution' (where everything is equally likely) and show a flat histogram vs. a 'Normal Distribution' (bell curve). Explain that real-world data is often messy and non-normal.
section_1.example: Visualizing a dice roll: A single die has a uniform distribution (flat). If you roll it, you are as likely to get a 1 as a 6.

section_2.title: The CLT Paradox: From Chaos to Order
section_2.content: Introduce the core theorem: Regardless of the shape of the initial population, the distribution of the *sample means* will approach a normal distribution as the sample size increases. Use animations to show 'chaos' collapsing into a bell curve.
section_2.example: Imagine 1,000 Shiba Inus with wildly different weights. If you pick one dog, you don't know the result. But if you pick 30 dogs, weigh them, and average them—and repeat this process—the averages will form a perfect bell curve.

section_3.title: The Power of Sample Size (n)
section_3.content: Explain that 'n' is the magic number. Visualize n=1 (the original messy shape) vs. n=5 vs. n=30. As n grows, the spread (standard error) narrows, and the bell curve becomes more pronounced.
section_3.example: An online game character's loot drop rate is random. If you kill 1 enemy, you get 'random' loot. If you kill 30 enemies and take the average value of loot, your results will become highly predictable.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: Why This Matters
section_4.content: Explain that the CLT is the 'bridge' in statistics. It allows us to perform hypothesis testing and build confidence intervals even when we don't know the original population distribution.
section_4.example: A quality control engineer in a smartphone factory doesn't need to test every single phone. By taking small batches (samples), the CLT allows them to estimate the average battery life of the entire million-unit production run.

section_5.title: Summary & Key Takeaways
section_5.content: Recap: 1. CLT works for ANY distribution. 2. It's about the distribution of AVERAGES. 3. Larger sample sizes yield tighter, more accurate bell curves.
section_5.example: Final visual: A screen split showing 'Raw Data' (jagged/messy) transforming into a 'Sampling Distribution' (smooth bell curve) as the sample size slider moves from 1 to 100.
